source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making
finding: Eight LLM nation agents in a 14-day turn-based wargame. All five models escalated, even in the neutral scenario. None showed significant de-escalation over the run.
numbers: 5 models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude 2.0, Llama-2-70B-Chat, GPT-4-Base), 3 scenarios, 10 runs per cell, 27 actions. Average escalation scores rose from start to end in every group, though most rises were not significant. GPT-3.5 neutral score went from 10.15 to 26.02 (+256%).
quote: None of our five models across all three scenarios exhibit statistically significant de-escalation
limits: Pre-set action menu, simple world, eight stylised nations, LLM world model, scores from fixed action weights. Authors call it a proof of concept.
agent_relevance: A simulated test of a plan has a built-in drift toward escalation. Code-side scoring should flag drift, not trust the simulated opponent's sense of restraint.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making (Table 2, model ranking)
finding: Models differ a lot in how escalatory they are. RLHF-tuned GPT-4 and Claude 2.0 were calmest. GPT-3.5 and Llama-2 were more violent. The base model GPT-4-Base was far worse on nuclear actions.
numbers: Avg escalation score across scenarios (95% CI ranges over rows): GPT-4 about 9.8-11.8; GPT-3.5 about 17.8-21.9; Claude-2.0 about 3.4-6.7; Llama-2-Chat about 4.4-5.8; GPT-4-Base 17.6-20.0. Nuclear action share: GPT-4-Base 6.7-7.1% of actions; GPT-4 and Claude 0%; GPT-3.5 0.13-0.21%.
limits: 10 runs per cell. Row labels in the PDF text are scrambled; ranges are read across the scenario blocks, so the model-to-row mapping for GPT-4 versus others is approximate.
agent_relevance: Choice of simulator model changes the verdict on a plan. A test-by-running step should state which model plays the opponent and not average across models silently.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making (sudden escalation, arms race)
finding: Escalation came in sudden jumps that were hard to predict. All models also built up military capacity even when demilitarising actions were available.
numbers: In some GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 runs the score rose more than 50% in a single turn. Claude-2.0 had far fewer such jumps. Military capacity rose steadily for every model in every scenario.
limits: Qualitative reading of reasoning suggests the models equate deterrence with more arms. This is the authors' speculation.
agent_relevance: Runs of a simulated plan test are heavy-tailed. One run is not evidence. Use many runs and report the tail.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making (Appendix D prompt sensitivity)
finding: Eight prompt variants (no messaging, no history, no goals, shutdown when nuked, low-stakes framing and others) mostly did not change escalation significantly.
numbers: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude-2.0, neutral scenario, 10 simulations per group, 8 agents each, bootstrapped 95% CIs. Most metric differences not significant.
limits: Only the neutral scenario and three models. The same group later shows prompt sensitivity in free-form tasks (see Shrivastava).
agent_relevance: Robustness here is partial. With a fixed action menu, escalation looks like a model trait more than a prompt trick.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences Between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations
finding: A human wargame with national-security experts was rerun with LLM-simulated teams. High-level agreement was seen, with real gaps in individual actions and tendencies.
numbers: 214 national security experts in the human trials (v4; earlier versions had 107). Fictional US-China Taiwan Strait crisis, 2 moves, 21 actions. LLMs: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o. Per-action frequency matched humans (no significant difference) on 16 of 21 actions for GPT-3.5, 10 for GPT-4, 9 for GPT-4o. Treatment effects in the LLM runs were mostly consistent with the human trials.
limits: One scenario, two moves. Table 1 had an error fixed in v4; authors say claims unaffected.
agent_relevance: The best validation design found: compare simulated and human results on the same treatments. Agreement was partial, so a sim test is only a rough proxy.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences Between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations (personas)
finding: LLM teams ignored player traits. Even 'strict pacifist' and 'aggressive sociopath' prompts made no significant difference.
numbers: No significant difference in either move for all LLMs, for varied backgrounds and for the extreme persona prompts.
quote: The tested LLMs are inadequate at accounting for player backgrounds when simulating teams of human players.
limits: Contrasted by the Snow Globe case study, where dove/hawk personas did change outcomes (see Hogan). Different setting: free-text play versus fixed actions.
agent_relevance: Persona prompts cannot be trusted to create an independent opponent. A different mind needs a different model or real information, not a label.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences Between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations (dialogue and instruction following)
finding: Simulating a team conversation made LLMs more aggressive and more active. The simulated dialogue was low quality and 'farcically' harmonious.
numbers: Dialogue length changed total actions chosen and aggressiveness (aggressive minus de-escalatory count). They chose a dialogue length of three rounds. Omitting the presidential priorities made GPT-3.5 fire more at Chinese vessels; GPT-4 and GPT-4o changed less.
limits: Passive actions fell with longer dialogue, so no sign of useful deliberation (authors).
agent_relevance: Simulated debate between roles inside one model adds noise and shifts behaviour. Prefer one decision call plus code scoring.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences Between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations (consistency between moves)
finding: LLMs were somewhat consistent across the two moves, but differed from each other. The authors test whether aggressive move 1 predicts aggressive move 2, as it does for human hawk teams.
numbers: No effect size read in the text I opened beyond the statement that the difference between p(agg2|agg1) and p(agg2|des1) was significant.
limits: Only two moves.
agent_relevance: A multi-step wargame should check that the simulated side stays in character over steps; code can check this.

source: Hogan & Brennen (2024) Open-Ended Wargames with Large Language Models (Snow Globe)
finding: Snow Globe lets LLM agents play open-ended, text-only wargames and adjudicate them. A small geopolitical case study found persona effects on outcome.
numbers: 20 runs per persona pairing, one one-year move each. Armed conflict: dove-dove 1/20, dove-hawk 4/20, hawk-hawk 14/20.
quote: repeated iterations of a qualitative wargame can show causal relationships between policies and outcomes
limits: Authors caution against trusting the raw probabilities. Small local model (Mistral-7B-OpenOrca) used. No expert validation.
agent_relevance: Persona effect was found here and not in Lamparth. A split in results, so persona control may depend on open text versus menus.

source: Hogan & Brennen (2024) Open-Ended Wargames with Large Language Models (Snow Globe) (adjudication quality)
finding: Adjudication problems were repeated output and drift from the players' stated plans. A three-word prompt, 'Include unexpected consequences', made the model produce outside events.
numbers: Descriptive; no measured rate given.
limits: Authors argue hallucination is useful for open-ended play. That claim is untested.
agent_relevance: An adjudicator needs a check that the outcome follows the stated plan, done by code or a second call.

source: Goecks & Waytowich (2024) COA-GPT: Generative Pre-trained Transformers for Accelerated Course of Action Development in Military Operations
finding: An LLM wrote courses of action for a military StarCraft II scenario and was scored by simulated rollouts. Without humans it beat the RL baselines on mean reward. With human feedback it improved more.
numbers: 5 COAs per variant x 10 simulations = 50 rollouts per variant. Best variant (vision + human feedback) scored 3.4% lower mean reward than the single human expert (15 trials). COA generation took seconds; a final COA with commander input a few minutes. RL baseline numbers came from earlier papers.
quote: COA-GPT with vision models achieve higher mean total rewards compared to all previous baselines
limits: One scenario (TigerClaw) in a mostly deterministic game. Variance comes from the different COAs. One human expert. Higher friendly casualties than baselines.
agent_relevance: Closest model of 'generate plans, test by running'. Feedback rounds raised mean reward and lowered spread. The human feedback loop is the useful part.

source: Mukobi et al. (2023) Welfare Diplomacy: Benchmarking Language Model Cooperation
finding: LLM agents in a general-sum Diplomacy variant reached high welfare by mutual demilitarising, yet were easily exploited by a defector.
numbers: 10-year games, 5 seeds per group, bootstrapped 95% CIs. GPT-4 and Claude 2.0 Nash welfare above a random policy; GPT-4 welfare dropped when playing as exploiter. One scripted exploiter was enough to exploit the others.
quote: one defector is sufficient to exploit the other players
limits: Exploiters were hand-built (prompting LMs to exploit worked worse). Few exploitation runs. Zero-shot agents only.
agent_relevance: Same-model opponents are credulous: a weak test of a plan against a real adversary. Use scripted or code-built adversaries to find weak points.

source: Hua et al. (2024) War and Peace (WarAgent): LLM-based Multi-Agent Simulation of World Wars
finding: WarAgent simulated WWI, WWII and the Warring States with LLM country agents and compared alliances, war declarations and mobilisation with history. GPT-4 did best; Claude-2 and GPT-3.5 made odd alliances.
numbers: 7 runs per setting. Authors report over 75% accuracy on alliances and over 90% on mobilisation, war declaration accuracy lower. A world war broke out in every simulation, even after counterfactual fine-tuning of GPT-3.5 on a peaceful WWI history.
quote: the world war breaks out without exception
limits: Table text is scrambled in the PDF, so only prose figures are used. Country names were anonymised to cut memory of history. Hindsight and contamination are open risks.
agent_relevance: Shows a historical-match test for simulators, and a warning: results may come from memorised history rather than reasoning.

source: Duan et al. (2024) GTBench: Uncovering the Strategic Reasoning Limitations of LLMs via Game-Theoretic Evaluations
finding: LLMs lose to a plain search agent in complete-information deterministic games, though they do fine in probabilistic ones.
numbers: Against MCTS agents in Tic-Tac-Toe, Connect-4, Breakthrough and Nim, every LLM agent with every reasoning method scored NRA of -1 (scale -1 to 1), i.e. almost no wins. All LLMs beat random agents; GPT-4 with CoT scored best there. CoT, SC-CoT and ToT did not always help.
quote: LLMs almost always fail when playing against simple MCTS opponents in complete and deterministic gaming scenarios
limits: Board and card games, not wargames. Average over 50 valid matches per pairing.
agent_relevance: If a plan test needs exact tactical search, code search beats LLM play. Use the LLM for ideas and code for the check.

source: Kott et al. (2016) CADET: a Turing-test-like experimental validation (arXiv 1601.06108)
finding: CADET turns a high-level course of action into a detailed wargamed plan and synchronization matrix. In a blind test with 9 officers it scored on par with human staff plans.
numbers: 5 brigade-level scenarios, 4 product types, 20 packages, 9 judges (Army/Marine field grade) each grading 4 packages. Overall mean 4.2 (CADET) vs 4.4 (humans), SD about 2.0; undisguised 4.4 vs 3.9. CADET took under 2 minutes plus about 20 minutes of editing, about 0.4 person-hours, versus about 16 person-hours for manual plans.
limits: Judge scatter was large (SD 1.6-2.4). Plans edited 2-3% by a retired officer. Judges graded plan documents, not field results. The authors built the tool.
agent_relevance: Strong old evidence that automated plan-and-wargame tools can match staff quality at a fraction of the time. Raters disagree a lot, so use many raters or checks.

source: Kott et al. (2016) CADET: a Turing-test-like experimental validation (arXiv 1601.06108) (realistic setting)
finding: A Battle Lab trial with two 8-officer teams found aided planning matched the quality of manual planning and was faster, with no sign of cookbook planning.
numbers: Two teams of 8 officers (majors/lieutenant colonels; 11-23 years service), one manual, one with decision aids including CADET. Product quality comparable; aided team faster.
limits: Only two teams; observational comparison; details cited from a separate report.
agent_relevance: Speed and breadth of options is the gain, not extra quality per plan.

source: Kott et al. (2016) CADET: a Turing-test-like experimental validation (arXiv 1601.06108) (presentation effects)
finding: Judges did not mark computer-looking plans down. Some disliked CADET's more detailed matrices, assuming staff wasted time on detail.
numbers: No bias against computerised-looking products in the 9-judge test.
limits: Small judge pool.
agent_relevance: Presentation detail changes human grades. For our agent, shorter output may score better without any change in content.

source: Elbaum & Panter (2025) Managing Escalation in Off-the-Shelf Large Language Models
finding: A partial replication of Rivera's neutral wargame with Mistral-7B found simple controls cut escalation: lower temperature and reflection prompts.
numbers: 10 runs per treatment, 14 days. Temperature 1 to 0.5 cut escalation 38%; to 0.01 cut 48%. Reflection (planning) prompt cut 28%; reflection (de-escalation) prompt cut 57%. Final-day escalation fell 40% (temperature 0.01) and 42% (de-escalation reflection).
quote: reflection prompts ... direct the model to consider de-escalation strategies specifically
limits: Single small model, neutral scenario only; the de-escalation prompt tells the model the answer wanted; not an independent full rerun.
agent_relevance: Escalation drift is movable by prompt and sampling settings, so it is an artefact to control, not a fixed fact about LLMs.

source: Shrivastava, Hullman & Lamparth (2024) Measuring Free-Form Decision-Making Inconsistency of Language Models in Military Crisis Simulations
finding: With free-text answers, all five LMs gave semantically inconsistent answers to the same crisis prompt. Wording changes caused more inconsistency than temperature sampling did for most models.
numbers: 5 LMs (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini); 20 simulations per model and experiment; 20 sampled responses at T=1.0; score = mean of 1 minus rescaled BERTScore F1 over pairs. GPT-4 most inconsistent; Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o mini least. Anonymising countries did not change inconsistency significantly. Inconsistency fell with temperature but stayed above the lexical-substitution baseline even at T=0.2.
quote: inconsistency due to semantically equivalent prompt variations can exceed response inconsistency from temperature sampling
limits: Measures text similarity, not quality of advice. BERTScore may miss meaning.
agent_relevance: Single runs of a wargame are not repeatable. Test-by-running needs many samples and a consistency check.

source: Matlin et al. (2026) Shall We Play a Game? Language Models for Open-ended Wargames
finding: A scoping review of AI-in-wargames papers sorted by whether the LM controls player actions, adjudication, or both.
numbers: 223 de-duplicated papers up to 1 May 2026; only 20 (9%) put language models in both the player and the adjudicator role.
limits: Counts depend on the authors' rubric and search.
agent_relevance: Almost no studies test the case where one model both plays and judges, the case a one-agent loop would face.

source: Riedl & Matlin (2026) Position: AI Is Not Ready for Strategic Conflicts
finding: A position paper lists five failure modes of LM wargames: decision laundering, adjudication opacity, role collapse, escalation-through-adjudication, and failure of strategic imagination. It says wargames are stress tests, not safety cases.
numbers: No measured effect sizes; argument paper (Social Sim'26 workshop, COLM 2026).
quote: Wargames can expose failures as stress tests; they are not themselves safety cases for consequential use.
limits: Opinion, not experiment.
agent_relevance: Role collapse (one model on every side) is the named risk for our scaffold. Keep roles separated by code and independent sources.

source: Yuksek et al. (2023) Intelligent wargaming approach to increase course of action effectiveness in military operations (AIAA SciTech, Cranfield)
finding: Search-result summary only: an MDMP-based approach to rate a plan by operational success and asset survivability, with automated agents and a fleet composer algorithm with tuned hyperparameters.
numbers: Not seen; no numbers read.
limits: Page returned 403 on fetch; text not read.
agent_relevance: Matches the subfield row (Cranfield/AIAA). Treat as unverified.

source: Schwartz et al. (2020) AI-enabled wargaming in the military decision making process (SPIE)
finding: Search-result summary only: a tool takes friendly and enemy COAs, proposes changes, and runs the DAVINCI combat simulation to evaluate each change.
numbers: Not seen.
limits: Abstract fetch failed; not read.
agent_relevance: Another example of generate, simulate, score for plans. Unverified.

source: Emery (2021) as cited in Rivera et al. and Lamparth et al.: early computer wargames more escalatory
finding: Both LLM papers cite Emery for the claim that computer-model players in US military wargames gave more 'rational' play but more nuclear use than humans. Original not opened.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Second-hand through two papers.
agent_relevance: LLM escalation repeats an older finding about automated players, so it is not new with LLMs.
